# Love it or loathe it, the movie ‘Misaligned’ is provoking debate on AI

Featuring synthetic actress Tilly Norwood, the comedy has sparked discussion over whether AI is another art form, or has it gone too far?

Tilly Norwood appeared on the scene about a year ago and already has quite a resume.

The denim-dressed digital persona created by European AI production company Particle6 first arrived with an Instagram account and a portfolio of modeling shots, selfies and movie scenes — and without a backstory or a single shred of evidence of life beyond the screen.

Fast forward a few months, and Norwood had racked up offers to be represented by talent agencies and for red carpet appearances, mock movie trailers, music videos — including one where she rides an inflatable flamingo. The latest plot twist in her quick rise to fame? On July 5, 2026, Particle6 announced that Tilly would be starring in the film “Misaligned.” With development still underway, the release date hasn’t been shared yet. Particle6 publicist Michelle Waldron said production is expected to take about a year.

Norwood plays “an AI being with no body, no childhood, and no lived experience of her own.” In a somewhat ironic, full-circle moment, Tilly is starring as a version of herself.

References to Tilly as a human have ruffled some feathers, fueling the debate around the ethics of AI use in acting. Northeastern University London philosophy professor Brian Ball said calling Tilly an actor is “probably a misnomer.” After all, “actors are people — and she is not.”

So who is “she?” Or should that be “it,” given that Norwood exists as a collection of of pixels and code rather than flesh and blood?

Tilly’s Instagram posts don’t hide the fact that she is “made of data” and exists to showcase the technology that created her. She’s an avatar — AI with a face, tousled curls and a beige trenchcoat. “Misaligned,” in turn, is a feature-length demo exploring AI’s strengths and possible pitfalls.

Ball pointed out that this technology has plenty of both. The very title of “Misaligned” points to the so-called “alignment problem,” the potentially catastrophic result of unintended consequences of AI’s actions.

Plot-wise, “Misaligned” is your typical coming-of-age meets ghost-in-the-machine story — think Pinocchio with pink lip gloss and a ring light. Living “in the Cloud,” an Instagram teaser reads, Tilly has no experience of her own but has access to the collective memory of humankind, much like AI models themselves.

Northeastern University AI faculty fellow and animator Jason Donati described it as a “pretty standard Hollywood fish-out-of-water kind of trope.”

While she seems like the ultimate blank slate, Tilly has some core traits that evolve as she moves through different contexts, Particle6 producer Lottie Webb pointed out. At one point, a rogue bot from the dark web lures her into a self-exploration quest that results in some deep misgivings about her own identity — or lack thereof. Ironically, the unease about the missing core self almost starts to look like the kernel of one.

Donati observed that while “questioning your existence is nothing new to cinema,” putting those questions in the mouth of an AI bot is an original move. Particle6 is pushing the boundaries by sidestepping traditional computer generation (CG) or motion capture tools to end up with a life-like result without a human anywhere in the picture — not even a voice actor, he said.

“The challenge (was) continuity,” Webb told Northeastern Global News, “making sure Tilly feels like the same ‘person’ scene to scene … even though every frame is generated rather than captured once on a set.” To accomplish this, a team of specialists use “a mix of off-the-shelf, publicly available AI tools” along with custom workflows to achieve emotional consistency across the film.” Editors help ensure that comedic timing stays on point. “The AI generates the raw material, but knowing where a beat lands, where a pause should be a half-second longer, that’s still a human judgment call,” Webb explained.

Donati likened it to an artistic experiment that aims to create a believable depiction of reality in an entirely new way. “It’s a sort of canary in the coal mine,” he said. He also defines this new medium as a “natural evolution of the digital avatar” intended to look realistic. “So realistic, I think, that it’s throwing people off,” he said.

After all, looking human isn’t the same as being human — and plenty of people in the industry have been quick to point out the difference.

The September 2025 statement by the SAG-AFTRA actors’ union condemned the idea of agents representing Tilly, claiming that “creativity is, and should remain, human-centered.”

Likewise, executive director of the annual Independent Film Festival in Boston, Brian Tamm frowned on the idea of presenting Tilly’s shenanigans as acting, which could potentially replace real–life performance.

“The point of acting is to find emotions in yourself and bring them to the character you’re playing,” Tamm explained. ”How can you embody having your heart broken if you don’t have a heart?”

According to him, the best you get with AI is a simulation — and a rather flat one at that. Human nature can’t be “reduced to ones and zeroes” of the binary digital world and is “too unpredictable” for a computer to figure out. After all, he said, “that’s why we’re driven to art in the first place,” both as creators and audience members.

In the end, much like AI is here to stay, so is Tilly. As Donati said, “the technology is going to be utilized. We need to figure out the ethics behind it, and it’ll just be another tool in the tool belt.”

After all, Tilly questioning her true nature might work as a plot device, but making sure she doesn’t cross ethical lines is ultimately up to the humans behind the scenes.
